nameStory: The Boston Facelina gets its name from Boston, Massachusetts, where this sea slug was first scientifically described and studied. The genus name 'Facelina' comes from Latin, referring to the torch-like projections on its back that early naturalists thought resembled small torches or flames.
description: The Boston Facelina is a small, colorful sea slug that crawls along the ocean floor and rocky surfaces. These marine creatures are nudibranchs, which means 'naked gills' - they breathe through finger-like projections on their backs instead of having enclosed gills like fish. They typically grow to about an inch long and have a translucent body with distinctive club-shaped projections called cerata that stick up from their back. Their bodies are often pale or translucent with orange, red, or brown coloration in the cerata.

idTips.label: Cerata projections
idTips.description: Look for finger-like or club-shaped projections sticking up from the back - these feel soft and squishy if gently touched, and often have colorful tips that may appear orange or reddish

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: The main body appears see-through or milky white, allowing you to sometimes see internal structures through the skin

idTips.label: Rhinophores
idTips.description: Two horn-like sensory tentacles project from the front of the head, often wrinkled or ridged in texture and used for detecting chemicals in the water

idTips.label: Oral tentacles
idTips.description: Two smooth tentacles extend from near the mouth area, usually shorter than the rhinophores and used for feeling around while feeding

idTips.label: Crawling movement
idTips.description: Moves by gliding smoothly across surfaces using its muscular foot, leaving a slight slime trail behind

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically reaches about an inch in length when fully extended, roughly the size of your thumbnail

habitat: Boston Facelinias live in shallow coastal waters along New England's rocky shores, typically found crawling on rocks, seaweed, and pier pilings in the intertidal zone. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are often discovered in tide pools or under rocks during low tide. Look for them in depths from the low tide line down to about 30 feet, particularly around areas where their hydroid prey grows.

seasonality.spring: Active and more visible as water temperatures begin to warm, often found in shallow tide pools during spring low tides.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most commonly observed crawling on rocks and feeding. Warm water makes them more active and easier to spot.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may begin moving to slightly deeper waters as temperatures cool. Good time to find them under rocks and in protected crevices.
seasonality.winter: Less active and harder to find as they retreat to deeper waters or more sheltered locations to avoid harsh winter conditions.

funFact: Boston Facelinias are solar-powered animals! They eat tiny hydroids that contain symbiotic algae, and when they digest their prey, they actually keep the algae alive in their finger-like projections, allowing the algae to photosynthesize and share nutrients - essentially turning the sea slug into a living, crawling garden.
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other small nudibranchs in tide pools, but the Boston Facelina's distinctive club-shaped cerata with colorful tips set it apart from most others. Remember: if it looks like a tiny underwater cactus with colorful fingertips, it's likely a Facelina.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sea slugs,' nudibranchs like the Boston Facelina are actually more closely related to snails than to terrestrial slugs - they're essentially snails that have lost their shells through evolution. The term 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gills,' referring to their external breathing structures.
compareHints: Since the Boston Facelina is the only Facelina species commonly found in New England waters, compare it to other aeolid nudibranchs in the family Facelinidae. The Boston Facelina's relatively large size (up to an inch), translucent body, and distinctly club-shaped cerata with colorful tips help distinguish it from smaller, more slender relatives. Its cerata are also typically more robust and fewer in number compared to other aeolid species that may have numerous thin, hair-like projections.
